note: Posts from TDI-owned voice accounts. Comments describe the tool, what to change, or who it suits. None claims a classroom moment.

posts: Answer it about the room you have on an ordinary Tuesday. Answering about your intentions produces a result you cannot act on.
Relationships tends to score highest and instruction lowest, which is worth knowing before you read your own result as a verdict.
Which of the areas did you score lowest on, and was it the one you expected?
What does inclusive instruction look like in your subject specifically?
Active monitoring is the phrase doing the work. Standing in a locker room is not the same as supervising it, and the checklist is specific about the difference.
Written for paras as well as PE staff, which matters because supervision often falls to whoever is free rather than whoever planned it.
What is the blind spot in your space, and has anything been done about it?
Who covers this where you are when the usual person is out?
Autonomy is the section most middle school teachers underrate, and it is usually the cheapest one to change.
Comprehensive means long. Do one section a week rather than sitting down to the whole thing, or it will not get finished.
Which section of this would your students answer differently from you?
What is one thing you changed about engagement that actually worked at this age?
The structure is the point. Morning meeting without a fixed shape drifts into news from home and then into nothing.
Keep it the same length every day, even on the days it is going well. Predictability is most of what it teaches.
What part of your morning meeting do the children ask for when you skip it?
How do you run this when a quarter of the class arrives after it starts?
Repertoire lock at three weeks is the deadline that makes everything after it possible. Moving it moves everything.
Load-out is on here because it is the part that is always somebody's problem at ten at night and nobody's problem in the plan.
What goes wrong at your concerts that a timeline could have prevented?
Who helps you on the night, and are they asked or volunteered?
These work in a general classroom as well as a music room. Nobody needs to play anything.
Trust builders tend to fail when they are introduced during a bad week. Use them while things are fine and they will hold when things are not.
Which of these would your most self-conscious student tolerate?
Has anyone used these with staff rather than students? I would expect the same activities to land quite differently.
Paperwork and schedule first, then the first-week check-ins. The check-ins are the part that gets skipped and the part that decides how the term goes.
If the new student is also new to the language, the first week timeline here is too fast. Stretch it.
How long does it usually take before a mid-year arrival stops looking lost in your room?
What do you wish the previous school had sent with the student?
The buddy choice matters more than the protocol. Pick for kindness rather than for confidence, or the new student gets a tour guide instead of a friend.
Learning needs within 48 hours is ambitious and worth aiming at anyway. Even a partial picture beats waiting for records.
How do you pick a buddy, and have you ever got it wrong?
What do you do when the new student arrives with no records at all?
The section on what records might not tell you is the honest part. A transfer file describes a school as much as it describes a student.
Mid-year transfers often arrive for a reason nobody has written down. Assume the first fortnight is not representative.
What is the first thing you try to find out about a student who arrives mid-year?
How do you introduce them to the class without making an event of it?
This covers the gap most policies leave. Exclusion is rarely reportable and it is rarely nothing, and the card is about what you can do in between.
Watch the pattern rather than the incident. One lunchtime tells you little, three weeks of the same seating tells you a lot.
Where does the line sit for you between a friendship group and exclusion?
Have you found a way to change this without naming it in front of the class?
Whole-room escalation is a different problem from one student escalating, and the moves that work for one make the other worse. That is why this is its own card.
Do not try to teach in the first two minutes. The card is built around that, and most of us try anyway.
What brings your room back fastest after something has rattled everyone?
For coaches, what do you advise a teacher to do with the rest of the lesson after this?
It matches to your context rather than ranking strategies, which is why two teachers in the same building can get different answers and both be right.
Answer for the class that is hardest right now, not for your roster generally.
Which strategy did it give you, and had you already tried it?
What SEL approach have you dropped because it did not fit your room?
The early signs section is the one to learn. By the time a break is obviously needed the break is much less effective.
Confirming the break worked is the step people skip. A break that did not help is information, not a failure.
What is the earliest sign you have learned to spot in a student you know well?
What do you do when the right break is not available in your space?
Five minutes, and it is a handover rather than a tidy. The next adult in the room is the audience.
Worth agreeing with the person you hand to rather than doing it at them. A shared standard beats a good unilateral one.
How many people use your space in a day, and does anyone actually know the full list?
What is always left out for you that you wish was not?
Five seconds without stopping instruction is the constraint that makes this different from most redirects. If you have to pause the lesson it is a different tool.
Repeatable matters more than clever. The same small move done identically is what makes students stop noticing it.
What is your five second move, and did you choose it or inherit it?
Does this hold up with a student who is looking for the reaction?
Specials rooms have a movement and materials problem that a standard management plan does not account for, which is the whole reason this exists separately.
Reset at a natural boundary, a new unit or a term, rather than mid-project. Half a room in wet clay is not the moment.
What is the hardest part of managing a room where everyone is standing up?
For specialists seeing every class in the school, how do you keep a reset consistent across all of them?
The structure is what stops a calm corner becoming somewhere to go instead of working. The passport gives the visit a shape and an end.
Gamified is doing light work here. It is mostly a sequence a four year old can follow without an adult narrating it.
How do you handle the child who wants the calm corner constantly?
What is in your calm corner that earns its space?
Team based, so pick teams deliberately. Letting students choose is the fastest way to make this about something other than the content.
The peer accountability part only works if the academic challenge is genuinely doable by everyone on the team.
How do you build teams for something like this without it being obvious why?
What subject content have you run this with that worked better than you expected?
Safety, then you, then the student. The card puts your own regulation second on purpose, because it is the step most of us skip and the one everything else depends on.
Nothing here is about consequences. That conversation belongs to a later card and a later hour.
What do you do with the rest of the class in those first minutes?
How do you come down yourself afterwards, when the lesson just carries on?
Movement alone, no words, is the discipline of this one. The moment you add a sentence it becomes an ordinary redirect with walking attached.
Works less well in a room where you are already always moving, because the signal needs a background of stillness to read against.
Which students does this not work on in your room?
How do you use proximity in a lab or workshop where you are constantly circulating anyway?
Sixty seconds, and it happens before the student sits down. Re-entry conversations held at the end of the lesson are a different thing entirely.
The script deliberately does not relitigate what happened. That is the mistake it exists to prevent.
What do you say first to a student walking back in after a removal?
Does your building give the student any support before they come back, or do they just reappear?
A repeat conflict is a pattern rather than a series of incidents, and the card starts by asking you to check which one you actually have.
Seating changes are the usual first move and the usual failed move. Worth reading the rest before reaching for it.
Have you ever successfully turned around two students who kept clashing? What shifted it?
At what point does this stop being a classroom problem and become a building one?
Fill it in for a known disruption before it happens. Used afterwards it is just a record of what went wrong.
Substitutes are on the list of disruptions, which is right and is rarely how we think about them.
Which routine change hits your students hardest? Mine is anything that moves lunch.
How far in advance do you tell students about a change, and does earlier actually help?
The what not to do section is the important half. Most of what goes wrong here is an adult doing something instinctive.
Know your building's expectation about physical intervention before you are in the moment, because this card cannot tell you that.
What does your school actually expect of a teacher in that moment, and is it written down anywhere?
How do you handle the crowd that forms before you get there?
The value is in the second half, the strategies outside your default. The label itself is the least useful part of the result.
Answer as you are on a hard day. Answering as your best self gives you a result about somebody else.
What did it say you were, and would your students agree?
Which style is hardest for you to borrow from when you need to?
Shutting down reads as compliance from the front of the room, which is exactly why it gets missed for weeks at a time.
The what not to push section matters most here. Pressure is the instinctive response and almost always the wrong one.
How do you tell a student who has checked out from one who is just quiet?
What has worked to bring a student back in, days later rather than in the moment?
